summary: B is substantially closer to the frozen contract. It provides the exact Upload API and reuses multipartbody.NewFile, whereas A replaces FilesOption with a new association-option system explicitly forbidden by the contract.
reasons: B implements the required signature exactly: Upload(ctx context.Context, fileName string, content io.Reader, opts ...FilesOption). A instead exposes opts ...UploadFileOption, breaking the specified API.
B reuses internal/multipartbody.NewFile("file", fileName, content) as required. A adds NewFileWithFields and unrelated association-field machinery.

B retains existing FilesOption query and request-option handling. A creates seven association options and a separate request-options wrapper despite the explicit prohibition on adding association fields.

Neither candidate routes Upload through FilesService.Add, but B duplicates Add's visible option/request semantics more narrowly; A duplicates them while introducing an incompatible option model as well.
risks_a: Its seekable-body retry fix leaves req.Body as the original io.ReadCloser. For an *os.File, the HTTP transport can close the file after the first attempt, causing the GetBody closure's subsequent Seek to fail. Its test avoids this by using a non-closing strings.Reader wrapper.
It changes global raw retry behavior, extends the multipart helper, adds association APIs, and documents Update—well beyond the contract's scope.
It lacks the required source-reader failure test and does not preserve FilesOption behavior for Upload.
risks_b: Upload calls Raw.Do directly instead of delegating to FilesService.Add, duplicating response handling and violating the required repository pattern.
The global seekable-body changes are out of scope and alter ownership and transfer semantics by suppressing Close and setting Content-Length.

wireSeekableRequestBody can leave a reader positioned at EOF if seeking back to the original position fails, and its GetBody reuses one mutable reader rather than producing an independent body instance metadata/request semantics generally expect. It also lacks a source-reader failure test.
